lesson_title: Soil, Passport and the Knife: How to Judge a Country
hook_text: One street has fibre and a stocked clinic. Five minutes away, water comes by tanker. Same town. Why?
clip_script: Take a Karoo town and stand on two of its streets, five minutes apart. On the first, the road is tarred, the taps run all day, the clinic keeps its fridge stocked with vaccines. On the second, the road is gravel and water arrives by municipal tanker twice a week. Development is the long work of bringing the second street up to the first — and read the list again: tar, taps, vaccines, teachers. Most of it is not simply money. Now the trap. A team totals one hundred and ten runs, and the scoreboard average says ten runs a player — healthy enough. Then you read the batting card: one player made ninety-one, and the other ten scraped nineteen between them. Same average, hollow team. That is South Africa's income story: a respectable average beside a Gini coefficient of about 0,63 — among the most unequal score-sheets on earth. So geographers carry two numbers everywhere: income per person, which sizes each slice of the cake, and the Gini, which tells you how the knife actually cut. Then one more score, the HDI report card with three subjects — health, education, income — where no country can cram the money subject and top the class. How much, how shared, how lived: judge any country with those three questions.
visual_style: A drone shot drifting between a tarred street and a gravel street of one Karoo town; a cricket scoreboard flipping from a healthy average to a batting card dominated by one name; a report card stamping three marks that merge into one HDI score over a map of South Africa.
mood: Grounded and eye-opening, closing on a challenge.
pacing: Slow two-street open, hard beat on the ninety-one reveal, brisk close through the three questions.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and judge any country's development with four numbers.
